analysis.one_liner: Requires drug companies to disclose biosimilar settlement deals to antitrust enforcers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee for the rest of the 115th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: When a generic-style copy of an expensive biologic drug (a "biosimilar") is developed, the brand-name maker and the copycat maker often settle their patent fights with private deals. Those deals can include payments or agreements that delay the cheaper copy from reaching the market. This bill would require both companies to file any such deal with the Justice Department's Antitrust Division and the Federal Trade Commission within 10 business days, with executives signing under penalty of perjury that they disclosed everything, so federal enforcers can police deals that squash competition.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and insurers who pay for high-priced biologic drugs, because the bill gives federal antitrust enforcers visibility into private deals that can keep cheaper biosimilars off the market, and lets the FTC and Justice Department penalize companies that hide those deals.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a brand-name biologic maker and any biosimilar applicant to file agreements about the manufacture, marketing, or sale of the products with the DOJ Antitrust Division and the FTC within 10 business days, and before first commercial marketing [S3].
Makes executives certify under penalty of perjury that filings include the complete agreement, any side deals, and any oral promises, closing the door on undisclosed side arrangements [S3].
Subjects violations to daily civil penalties recoverable by the United States or the FTC, and lets courts order compliance or other relief [S3].
The bill's stated purpose is to enhance competition for prescription drugs by increasing DOJ and FTC ability to enforce existing antitrust laws for biologic and biosimilar products [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic manufacturers, which would face new mandatory filings and perjury-certified disclosure of their settlement terms, and potentially higher exposure to antitrust enforcement over pay-for-delay-style deals.

drawbacks.text: The filing requirement covers a wide range of agreements about manufacture, marketing, or sale, so companies would face new compliance costs and legal risk even for deals that raise no competition concerns; the bill excludes only raw-material purchase orders, equipment contracts, employment deals, and packaging/labeling contracts [S3].
Mandatory disclosure of settlement negotiations could make companies more reluctant to settle patent disputes at all, potentially extending litigation over biosimilar products [S3].

The filings themselves are exempt from public disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act, so the bill gives enforcers information but does not directly give patients or the public visibility into the deals [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a modest transparency measure: it does not ban pay-for-delay deals or directly lower prices, but it hands the FTC and Justice Department the information needed to enforce antitrust laws that already exist, at a compliance cost borne by drug companies. The main limitation is that disclosure alone does nothing unless enforcers choose to act. It was narrow, low-cost, and uncontroversial on its face, which makes its quiet death in committee more notable than the substance of the bill itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat until the 115th Congress ended with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. John Sarbanes introduced the bill on July 23, 2018, joined by Rep. Johnson of Ohio, making the sponsorship bipartisan from the start [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S5].
Four days later it was referred to the Health Subcommittee, the last action of any kind on the bill [S5].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, with the bill still pending in subcommittee, so it died without a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name biologic manufacturers are better off because the bill died; their settlement agreements with biosimilar makers remain unreported to antitrust enforcers, and the status quo of private deals affecting drug competition is preserved.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan (one Democrat from Maryland and one Republican from Ohio), but no committee or floor votes were ever held, so the partisan shape of broader support and opposition is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would have forced them to file, under penalty of perjury, any agreements with biosimilar makers concerning the manufacture, marketing, or sale of their products, exposing pay-for-delay-style deals to antitrust scrutiny. Because these companies benefit from settlement terms that can delay cheaper copies of their drugs, their interest in this bill ran against patients paying high drug prices.

The bill targets agreements between biosimilar applicants and brand-name sponsors, and greater antitrust visibility into deals that sideline biosimilars supports their entry into the market. Cheaper biosimilars reaching patients is the mechanism by which ordinary people benefit.
